articles.title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
articles.summary: Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit less than two months ago, leaving thousands dead and missing.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Flash flood washes building complex in central Nepal By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 11 October 2026 
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said. 
Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing. 
A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex. 
Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing. 
Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar. 
Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies. 
The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. 
Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said. 
Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location." 
However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August. 
What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche. 
Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood. 
"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said. 
"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet." 
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.

articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Yvette Tan 
- Published 8 October 2026 
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries. 
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. 
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place. 
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. 
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter. 
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports. 
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement on Thursday that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions". 
"Despite Seoul's decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue - even if it takes time," he said. 
Earlier on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a statement it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly". 
- 
Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
- Published 11 January 2025 
- 
Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll 
- Published 7 May 
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive". 
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. 
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. 
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. 
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. 
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. 
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. 
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. 
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. 
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. 
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. 
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. 
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago -  why are they resuming now?
articles.summary: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey Bethea By Sheila Flynn Senior US reporter 
- Published 10 October 2026 
They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow. 
It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to spectators. 
By the execution time of 05:00, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000. 
That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70. 
The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream. 
Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner". The local sheriff had died four months earlier and his widow had become his unlikely replacement. 
She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was a hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death. 
That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in the US. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later. 
By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now. 
Image source, FPG/Staff/Getty Image caption, 
Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the US 
A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan , who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. 
The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be livestreamed. 
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. 
University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked. 
"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC. 
He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining - it was at 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%. 
"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said. 
It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in. 
With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment... bring your popcorn, invite your friends". 
Figure caption, 
Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa Pike 
Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream. 
"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up... to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific." 
Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's death in 2002, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap. 
The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution. 
"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. 
"Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific." 
But the polarisation and rhetoric in US politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University. 
"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. 
"So it's not like they're cheering a public execution - they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'" 
Figure caption, 
Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? 
Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong. 
Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said surveys point to a declining appetite for violence in the US. 
"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people." 
"I think it's this: a public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country." 
The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday. 
US Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned and said he would not watch it if it were livestreamed. 
Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. 
He did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution. 
"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

articles.title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
articles.summary: A flash flood at the Budhi Gandaki River has swept away several buildings and bridges, two months after catastrophic floods hit the country.
articles.full_text:
Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal 
Close 
A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal. 
The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed. 
It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. 
Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river. 
Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’ 
The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals. 
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week. 
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries. 
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”. Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket 
Read more 
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU. 
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China . 
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. 
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints. 
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said. 
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too. skip past newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen 
The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG 
Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.” 
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin. 
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”. 
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes. 
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal 
Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs 
The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. 
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers. 
The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday. Read more 
“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place. 
China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs. 
Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles. 
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that. 
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said. 
“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart. 
Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition. 
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared. 
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe. 
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday. 
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”. 
It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”. 
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

Mao’s Last Dancer Li Cunxin on his long-awaited follow-up: ‘I don’t think my publisher expected it to take 14 years!’ 
Tim Byrne 
As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland Ballet 
- 
Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email 
S ome people live such extraordinary lives that a single autobiography simply won’t suffice. Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director of Queensland Ballet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans. 
“Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. But then I was offered the job at Queensland Ballet and I had to dedicate all my time to that. I don’t think they were expecting [the sequel] to take 14 years!” 
His second memoir, The Lucky Son, takes up precisely where Mao’s Last Dancer left off: as Cunxin and his ballet dancer wife Mary fly to their new lives at Houston Ballet under the directorship of Ben Stevenson. That outline of the proposed book on China can be glimpsed under the surface of this one, like a palimpsest; Cunxin’s six brothers’ lives are sketched, and a fascinating portrait of a country lifting itself from abject poverty to world superpower emerges. 
View image in fullscreen 
Li Cunxin and Mary McKendry in Ben Stevenson’s Sleeping Beauty in 1988. Photograph: Houston Ballet 
“One of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all times,” Cunxin says. “Don’t think about the past, just concentrate on what is ahead.” That grit kept her children alive and was instrumental in shaping Cunxin’s dogged, highly ambitious personality. 
Determination runs in the family. Mary was a deeply respected dancer herself, a career she sacrificed when she and Cunxin discovered their daughter Sophie was born profoundly deaf. “We were so fearful that Sophie would miss out on so much,” Cunxin says. “Music and dance and all the magical things.” 
Mary immediately left the world of ballet (she would return years later as ballet mistress at Queensland Ballet) to teach Sophie to talk. “Mary was incredible,” Cunxin recalls. “She gave everything to the task.” 
One one hand, it was a complete success. Sophie was fitted with a bionic ear (then known as a cochlear implant) and thrived; she embraced dance, had a successful education and excelled in the workplace. Cunxin and Mary assumed they’d done all that was needed. 
View image in fullscreen 
‘To be a leader of any kind takes vision. I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet.’ Photograph: David Kelly/The Guardian 
But then in 2015, Sophie sent an email to her parents that shocked and devastated them. Sophie expressed frustration at her parents for wanting their daughter to hear; she felt she’d come halfway to meet their world, but they had not met hers. They had not even bothered to learn sign language. Her “deafness was her birthright”, Cunxin writes in the book. Now, he says, Sophie “is a kind of ambassador between the hearing and deaf communities”. And he and Mary have begun learning Auslan. 
Cunxin’s dance career was so exemplary – moving from the Beijing Dance Academy to Houston Ballet, and then to principal artist at Australian Ballet – he could have been forgiven for hanging up his pointe shoes and walking into a lucrative position in a stockbroking firm. Indeed, that’s exactly what he did. An unsuccessful tilt at the artistic directorship of Australian Ballet (the role eventually went to David McAllister) utterly crushed him, and it seemed for a few years he would never return to the world of professional ballet. 
Of course, that wasn’t how it panned out: despite being burned by that failure, Cunxin reluctantly put his name in the hat when Queensland Ballet were looking for their next artistic director. That tenacity and resolve was once more poured into the theatre. 
“To be a leader of any kind takes vision,” Cunxin says. “I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet. But you also have to be a good communicator, because you need to inspire others to join in your vision.” And you need to apply yourself, which wasn’t such an issue for someone trained at Beijing Dance Academy, with its brutal rehearsal regime and exacting standards. 
One of the delights of The Lucky Son is the way it tracks some of our favourite characters from Mao’s Last Dancer, including The Bandit, Cunxin’s bestie at the Beijing Dance Academy; his gorgeous instructor Teacher Xiao; and his astonishing mum and dad, Niang and Dia. There are echoes in the events too: Stevenson’s trip to Queensland to watch his protégé mount Cinderella recalls the unforgettable moment in Mao’s Last Dancer when his parents leave China for the first time to see their son dance and the audience gives them a standing ovation. 
View image in fullscreen 
Cunxin at the Thomas Dixon Centre, home of the Queensland Ballet. Photograph: David Kelly/The Guardian 
Central to Cunxin’s success at Queensland Ballet – where he oversaw a massive improvement in standards and built a stunning new home for the company, the Thomas Dixon Centre – were the lessons he learned from his time away from ballet, when he was a stockbroker: “I learned so much from the business world – when we had to approach donors for money, I could speak their language.” Relationships with Elisabeth Murdoch and the Ian Potter Foundation came in handy, and he and Mary also contributed some money of their own. It’s now a world-class organisation. 
Looking back on his life now, Cunxin feels an overwhelming sense of “gratitude, for the opportunities I was given and the people and artists who shaped me”. The Lucky Son concludes on stage – hardly surprising, given so many of the key moments in Cunxin’s life have been there – but this time it is in Switzerland, where he was awarded ballet’s most prestigious award, the Prix de Lausanne, in 2025. Best Australian books out in October: Magda Szubanski, delicious recipes and a picture book ‘masterpiece’ 
Read more 
After a few years of serious health issues (Mary is a cancer survivor and Cunxin has a major heart condition), the couple are increasingly happy to chill. “Our health has forced us to slow down,” he says with the emphasis on forced, as if there were no way they would slow down on purpose. “I worked very hard for two years on this book – it’s been all-consuming. So yes, I am enjoying taking things a little slower.”
Is he confident that ballet will survive the coming AI tsunami, given how hard the art form is to perfect and how much time and effort is required? “I am worried, but I do think ballet is special,” he says. “When people come to see ballet, they are blown away by the artistry, the physicality and the music. I think it’s more important than ever to connect people.”

EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war
Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné says bloc will support 46 strategic projects including lithium and rare earths plants 
The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China , the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects. 
Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc. 
“We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.” 
The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn). 
They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China , with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc. EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China 
Read more 
“We’re pulling out all the stops to move as quickly as possible. The primary objective is the targets set by law, and beyond that, there’s a geopolitical challenge that could catch up with us very quickly,” said Séjourné. 
“Mines are opening, factories are being built, financing agreements are being signed, and a European value chain is emerging,” Séjourné added. 
Amid some scepticism over the EU’s ability to meet its 2030 targets to reduce dependencies on China, Séjourné cited three “emblematic” projects which have previously been identified as strategic, earmarking them for accelerated permits. 
These included a rare earths plant near Pau in south-western France. The Carester plant, which is expected to be up and running in late 2026, produces dysprosium and terbium, “two raw materials for which we are almost entirely dependent on China”, used in magnets for electric vehicles and offshore wind turbines. 
“This single project could account for about 15% of global production of these oxides. That is no small feat,” Séjourné said. 
He also name-checked a gallium plant in Greece which is already up and running. 
The third, Keliber, a lithium extraction and processing plant in Finland, is also operational after €150m support from the European Investment Bank. 
The 46 projects are the second batch of initiatives to receive flagship status since the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024, which legally mandates the European Commission to reduce the bloc’s dependency on foreign countries. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
The EU hopes to follow in the footsteps of Japan, which has reduced dependency on China for rare earths to 60% from 90% since 2011, when Beijing prohibited exports of about 20 materials to Japan, claiming they were being used for military purposes. 
Although the flagship status does not bring the projects direct funds, it enables accelerated permitting, and help in mobilising funds. 
However, there has been criticism in industry within the EU that the scheme is not strong enough to deliver targets to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the bloc’s needs by 2030. 
The French lithium refiner Viridian Lithium, which received EU strategic status in 2025, went into judicial liquidation in March this year. 
Earlier this year, a group of 23 of the 60 projects designated strategic in 2025 wrote to the European Commission calling for more action to “urgently unlock projects, particularly those working towards final investment decision which face acute liquidity and market pressure and ​immediate jeopardy”. 
Séjourné said member states had unlocked €1bn for six of the projects, with the European Investment Bank providing another €660m for eight projects.

‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives
Whether on the frontline in Ukraine or skate parks in Soweto, the genre is still a vital outlet for disaffected people everywhere. Here, musicians explain how they rage against the machine 
Ukraine: ‘I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline’
Andriy Zholob , vocalist/guitarist , Beton : When MTV arrived in Ukraine , I heard Nirvana, the Offspring, Bad Brains, Social Distortion and thrash metal, and realised that all this started from punk rock. Our drummer and I were in a ska-punk band first, but when our vocalist became pregnant we started Beton in 2017 and played lots of festivals. 
Everything changed with the invasion. In 2022, I started military service as a surgeon on the frontline. We were attacked many times and on at least four occasions I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline and every evening we’d play just to relax. At one point, my commander gave me eight days off to record a battle song for our brigade and Beton did a cover of the Clash’s London Calling – Kyiv Calling – to raise money for the Ukrainian resistance. I wanted to use punk rock to stand against evil. 
Watch the video for Kyiv Calling by Beton. 
I finished my service two years ago, quit medicine and now work with veterans, many of whom come to our gigs. There are guys and girls with prosthetics, slam dancing, singing along and everything. It’s a real moment of punk rock unity. We play two or three shows every month, but I like to spend time in the mountains. Although I play punk rock, sometimes I need silence. 
Morocco and Spain: ‘People would tell me: you love Satan’
Nao, vocalist, Taqbir : In the Muslim community of Morocco , where I come from, the punk look is not accepted. For a long time, I had to perform anonymously, with my face covered, in case people recognised me and wanted to hurt me. Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted. Even in Spain, where I live now, I felt isolated as an immigrant and as a woman who did crazy things to my hair. People would tell me: “You love Satan.” 
View image in fullscreen 
‘Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted’ … Taqbir. Photograph: Alejandra Núñez 
I heard Crass when I was 13. They were the first band I heard where I recognised myself in the lyrics, because I felt oppressed by religion. Then through chatting with friends online, I discovered more. I’d go to shows in Madrid, take off my hijab and wear makeup. It was a double life that meant I finally felt free to be myself, but for a long time punk cost me my relationship with my family. 
Being in Taqbir really helped. I was very angry, so fronting the band was like a cure for this rage. People seem to connect with the rawness. We’ve played in north Africa and the UK and my dream is to be able one day to play in Morocco. Punk has helped me see that things don’t have to be black and white: people can be punk and Muslim and gay. Although there’s anger, our message is positive. If you’re feeling oppressed or that you cannot be yourself in this society, Taqbir are for you. 
South Africa: ‘Being from Soweto automatically makes you political’
Abdula Skink, vocalist, Twenty One Children : A lot of kids in Johannesburg got into punk because there were no jobs or infrastructure for us. I grew up in a hip-hop house, but found bands such as Suicidal Tendencies and Black Flag through video games and older friends who skated. Punk just flicked all these switches in my head. Our guitarist, Thula, used to play in TCIYF, the first all-black punk band in South Africa . When we started our band in 2023, I was an assistant teacher for 21 autistic kids, so that became our name. I was also 21, so it felt like a lucky number. 
Being from Soweto automatically makes you political. All the great revolutionaries – Hugh Masekela, Nobel prize winners, Desmond Tutu and so on – came from here. Our motto is: if something isn’t true, we won’t sing about it. Our song Scab is about a time I was stopped by police because I was skating through a historically Afrikaans/white area. I had green hair and the policeman was like: “You’re on drugs.” He ripped my Suicidal Tendencies T-shirt, dropped my laptop from my bag on the street and tried to take my skateboard. I wasn’t doing anything illegal. They were just fucking with me. Mostly, we try to make a difference in our communities. Thula built the first DIY skate park in Soweto; we’ve done charity shows for orphanages and such. For us, punk is not so much a livelihood but a way of life. 
India: ‘We were bombarded with threatening messages’
Aditya Naik, vocalist/guitarist, Punk on Toast : I grew up listening to Bad Religion, NOFX, the Sex Pistols and the Clash and saw a satirical commentary about our times, so I started the band when I was 17 so I could talk about what was happening around us. In India , you see cruelty or injustice on every corner, so we don’t relate to mainstream music, which ignores this. 
View image in fullscreen 
‘There’s a lot of oppression of artists’ … Punk on Toast. Photograph: Courtesy of Punk on Toast 
At the moment, there’s a lot of oppression of artists. After our song Modified talked about what the right wing are trying to do with us, we were bombarded with threatening messages online. People went through all our profiles, trying to find our phone numbers, where we live, our employers. It felt like being molested. Although we’ve had coverage in Rolling Stone India, the punk scene mostly flies under the radar, but that means we’re freer to sing about what we want. 
We took part in the recent Cockroach protests in Mumbai , which alerted people to how things are and got everybody out on the street. Before that, India felt like a small elite club where everyone else is the “cockroaches”, so it was like seeing a phoenix: hope. The punk scene is growing, with our friends Pacifist and Emergency Trigger and bands such as the Light Years Explode and the Riot Peddlers. It’s more about documenting our times and standing for what’s right rather than selling lots of records, but punk rock gave me the greatest superpower: question everything. 
Brazil: ‘Under a military dictatorship, there were kids brave enough to play with passion and fury’
Henrike Baliu , vocalist, Blind Pigs and Armada : When the original UK punk explosion happened in 1977, my dad was a naval engineer stationed in Southampton. He saw the Boomtown Rats performing Lookin’ After No 1 on Top of the Pops and told the guy in the record shop: “Give me everything you’ve got” – which meant the Sex Pistols, Generation X and so on. 
Listen to São Paulo City by Armada. 
Years later, when I was 12, I played some of my dad’s records to my friends and they told me about the punk scene in Brazil . Bands such as Ratos de Porão, Inocentes and Cólera sang about life under a military dictatorship, which Brazil was in the 80s. People were disappearing or being murdered, so it blows my mind that under a dictatorship with virtually zero news, poverty and police brutality there were kids with spiky hair brave enough to wear fake leather jackets and play with passion and fury. Those bands were pioneers who paved the way for us. 
Blind Pigs were probably the biggest punk band in Brazil over the last 30 years, but now I’m focused on Armada. We are bilingual and sing in Portuguese and English. When we recorded our English language album, Tales of Treason, the country was going through another crazy time politically and the right wing were on the rise again. With the music, I wanted to warn people to learn from history: “Dudes, you don’t want that again.” 
Latvia: ‘On stage I let out all my anger’
View image in fullscreen 
‘On stage, I let out all my anger’ … Evisa Petrovska of Depustūtes. Photograph: Katrīna Līva Dalbiņa 
Evisa Petrovska, vocalist, Depustūtes : In high school, I didn’t really like pop, so I got into metal, but I felt it was missing lyrical depth, so punk really resonated. Ramones and the Sex Pistols sang about the same stuff that made me mad or frustrated. The Dead Kennedys’ political commentary really connected and then I discovered riot grrrl. As I got older, I realised there was a punk scene here in Riga and a whole community of people like me. 
There’s so much going on in the world – I’ll never run out of topics and writing and singing in the band never gets boring. On stage, I let out all my anger. Whether I’m running or crawling on the floor, it’s just pure emotion. Singing in Latvian makes it easier to sing about local politics. Lately, we’ve been addressing how people who actually benefit society aren’t getting paid as well as those who aren’t, but I sing about societal norms and stereotyping. 
Our song Mrs Pieklājība (Mrs Polite) starts, in a mocking way: “I love listening to men and being obedient.” It was inspired by people telling me “you should smile more” or “women don’t dress like that”. There’s always been at least two women in the band, but most people are really supportive. I love inspiring other girls’ lives. A lot of them come up after shows and say: “That was so inspiring. I wish I could speak as freely as you.” 
China: ‘Our albums were confiscated and our work was taken offline’
Wu Wei, vocalist, SMZB : Wuhan and Beijing were the first cities in China to have punk music. I founded the first punk band in Wuhan in 1996 after falling in love with tapes that my friends sent me from the US – initially the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Ramones and then bands with other styles, such as US Bombs, Suicide Machine and Rancid. Through punk, I finally found a way to express myself. Although the scene is still quite small, we were one of the first bands to go on national tours, which influenced the development of punk in other cities. We sing about the environment we operate in: political aspects and things I’ve witnessed in daily life under the system in China. 
Watch the video for Ten Thousand Ways to Rebel by SMZB. 
A few years ago, the authorities prohibited us from performing. Some albums were confiscated, our work was taken offline and our record company was forced to terminate our contract. Despite this, our audiences have a wide age span and range from other punks and bands to art workers, students and ordinary wage-earners. Punk has brought me so many things, from running the bar Wuhan Prison to my personal life. I’ve now settled in the UK with my family, but frequently return to Wuhan for rehearsals and recording. SMZB just released a bilingual album, When the Party Is Over, for our 30th anniversary. Punk has given me my life. 
Greenland: ‘I’m 38, a father, still have my piercings and still consider myself a punk’
Jenseeraq Olsen, vocalist/guitarist, Uummat : We have a running joke with Iceland that they are green and we are ice, so most people live on the coast. I was in Denmark for a festival recently and realised that there were more people there – 70,000 – than the entire Greenlandic population. Punk is very much a minority interest here, but I was always rebellious when I was young and didn’t like the mainstream pop my friends were into. ‘I knew it was over for us’: the bands who got left behind when punk exploded 
Read more 
After I saw an advert for Blink-182’s Enema of the State album after the movie American Pie, I realised they were the band I’d been searching for. I was teased for having multicoloured hair and ripped clothes, but Blink were a big influence on Uummat, which means “heart”. We were different from other bands in Greenland and people connected with it: we’ve played to 2,000 people. 
I’ve never really written political songs, but Trump’s threat to annex Greenland has made a lot of people emotional, stressed and nervous, which I’m sure will come out in the music. I’m 38, a father and manage a youth centre now, but Blink resonate as much as they did when I was 15. I still have my piercings and I still consider myself a punk. Meanwhile, my 11-year-old son listens to the same music and plays guitar like me. He thinks labels like “punk” are for adults, but he likes the word, so he’ll probably follow in my footsteps.
